title: Giving £2 a day to people in the Amazon helps protect rainforest, pilot project finds | Amazon rainforest | The Guardian
snippet:
A river snaking through a forest
The experiment involved three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region. Photograph: Martín Mejía/AP
The experiment involved three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region. Photograph: Martín Mejía/AP
Giving £2 a day to people in the Amazon helps protect rainforest, pilot project finds
Researchers say almost 90% of participants in unconditional basic income scheme in Peru adopted environmentally beneficial practices
Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.00 BST
Last modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.02 BST
Share
A pioneering project to provide Indigenous people in the Peruvian Amazon with an unconditional basic income has contributed to the protection of the rainforest, according to a study.
The analysis from the University of Bath is expected to contribute to a growing debate about the role of direct payments to communities that maintain globally important ecosystems.
A two-year pilot managed by the UK-based charity Cool Earth gave 211 people in three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region six cash transfers of 1,032 Peruvian soles each – roughly equivalent to £2 a day – to spend as they wished.
Over the course of the trial, researchers found almost 90% of participants adopted environmentally beneficial practices, such as collective reforestation, restoration of critical water sources and reductions of forest burning.
They also noted a reduction in food insecurity, which can sometimes prompt forest people to start logging or become involved in environmental crimes. Households unable to afford nutritious food fell from 73% to 26%.
Another reported benefit was reduced migration, with the share of participants forced to leave their homes to find work falling from 43% to 18%. Researchers said this allowed more people to remain and protect the forest.
Dr Nick Langridge, a co-author of the report, said: “The findings suggest that when communities have greater security and autonomy, they are better able to protect the ecosystems they depend on.”

Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together.
Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."
The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.
With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.
Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.

"In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group.
The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said.
Musk, chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects.
Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations.

Image shows the water tower in Springfield, Ohio

In this closely fought midterm election campaign, the small town of Springfield, Ohio, has become a symbol of modern America. But it is a symbol that changes dramatically depending on who is describing it.
To President Donald Trump, Springfield crystallises America's problems due to years of unchecked immigration. He once echoed a false claim that Haitian immigrants were eating pets here. Today, he says his mass deportation drive means its people are "getting their town back".
But to others, Springfield represents a well-known cycle in the story of modern America. The decline of traditional industry, followed by a spike in immigration fuelled by cheap housing and low-paid labour. It is a familiar tale across the country.

Bel, according to a family friend, then received a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which gives vetted individuals the right to live and work in the United States.
TPS usually lasts 18 months but is routinely rolled over, often for years, if the danger remains in the affected country.

Some lump sum pension payments to families are only tax-free if made within two years of a scheme being told of the member’s death.
MPs are now voicing fears that severe delays in the administration of the civil service pension scheme, which is run by the outsourcing company Capita, could push some families over that threshold. They would then be hit with a tax bill calculated at the recipient’s personal rate.

Before 24 July, a person I will call R was preoccupied with the ordinary routines of teenage life: experimenting with makeup, grumbling over mathematics homework and hanging out with friends at a tea stall.
That month, as the fever of student protests spread across the country, the 15-year-old watched on her phone as young people poured into Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, demanding education reform. She went too. But an 11-second video clip from the protest site, in which she made crude and profane remarks about the prime minister, Narendra Modi, upended her life.
“I feel like a criminal, as if I murdered someone,” R said in her first interview about life since the backlash. “I didn’t get a chance to make amends. In my own country, I am being treated like an enemy.”
It’s been 86 days since that protest, but R doesn’t leave home over safety concerns, trapped in the reality the ordeal created.
The summer agitation had for weeks demanded the ousting of the then-education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, over repeated examination paper leaks. But after a violent police crackdown on a student march the anger spilled over to the Modi government.

Breaking news alerts on the BBC News website
Whenever you come to the BBC News website on a tablet or computer, you'll get notified of the latest breaking news in the 'breaking news banner' which automatically appears at the bottom of your browser window.
The banner will disappear when you click on it, dismiss it or visit another page.
Add BBC breaking news alerts to your BBC News app
Push notifications are available to users of smartphones and tablets who download the BBC News app, allowing you to receive breaking news alerts. When a push notification is received it will pop up on your screen similar to a text message, regardless of whether or not the app is open at the time. Depending on your settings the alert may also be accompanied by a sound. Tapping the notification will load the corresponding story in the app when it is available. snippet:
US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin
Stephen Hubbard, an elderly man wearing a light green jumper, sits handcuffed in a glass cubicle in the courtoom.Image source, Reuters
Image caption,
Stephen Hubbard pictured in a Moscow courtroom as he was sentenced in 2024
ByMaia Davies
Published
21 October 2026, 10:22 BST
Updated 20 minutes ago
Russia has released a 74-year-old American citizen who was jailed for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine, as President Vladimir Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg for talks.
Stephen Hubbard has been taken to Pulkovo Airport, Putin said during the meeting early on Wednesday.
President Donald Trump later said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary".
Hubbard was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024. He was accused of serving in a defence unit in Izyum, Ukraine, when he was captured by Russian forces shortly after Moscow's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Writing on social media after Russian state media reported the release, Trump said it had followed a request he "made directly" to Putin last week.
Some other releases of detained Americans from Russia have been obtained through prisoner swaps.
Trump also appeared to defend his recent decision to suspend sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to come into force, writing that "if sanctions would have been placed", negotiations for Hubbard's release "would have come to a complete and total halt".
The US State Department had previously classified Hubbard, from Michigan, as "wrongfully detained" and the US president had suggested on Tuesday that his release may be imminent.
"Watch what happens," Trump told reporters, "we have been focused on Hubbard".
CBS News, the BBC's US media partner, reported that Hubbard had been in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment.

In 1368, he proclaimed the Ming dynasty, adopted the era name Hongwu, and expelled the Yuan from China proper. During his 30-year reign, he restored stability after decades of war, strengthened state institutions, promoted agriculture, and maintained a disciplined army while seeking to limit civilian suffering. The Hongwu Emperor (21 October 1328 – 24 June 1398), personal name Zhu Yuanzhang, was the founding emperor of the Ming dynasty of China, reigning from 1368 to 1398. Born into a peasant family in Anhui, Zhu grew up amid famine, epidemics, and unrest under the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty. Orphaned at 16, he briefly lived as a novice monk before joining the Red Turban rebels in 1352. Rising rapidly, he captured Nanjing in 1356, established a regional regime, and defeated rival rebels. In 1368, he proclaimed the Ming dynasty, adopted the era name Hongwu, and expelled the Yuan from China proper. During his 30-year reign, he restored stability after decades of war, strengthened state institutions, promoted agriculture, and maintained a disciplined army while seeking to limit civilian suffering. He died in 1398 and was succeeded by his grandson, the Jianwen Emperor, who was overthrown in 1402 by Zhu Di, later known as the Yongle Emperor. (Full article...)

title: Author Helen Fielding launches award to find the next Bridget Jones's Diary - BBC News
snippet:
Author Helen Fielding launches award to find the next Bridget Jones's Diary
Renée Zellweger (left) and Helen Fielding pictured together while attending the Bridget Jones Scenes in the Square statue unveiling at Leicester Square, London in 2025Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding (right) alongside film star Renée Zellweger
ByPaul Glynn
Culture reporter
Published
2 hours ago
Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding has launched a new prize aimed at discovering funny diary writers from the north of England, saying opportunities across the UK are "very uneven".
West Yorkshire-born Fielding, who penned Bridget's famous diary as well co-writing the film adaptations, has set up the Bridget Jones Prize, external with charity New Writing North.
The award will go to the person who submits the funniest 1,000-word piece of first-person writing.
Speaking at an event for the Independent, which first published Bridget's diary in 1995, Fielding said the spread of opportunity for writing in the UK is "very uneven", adding: "There's much more opportunity in the south than in the north, where I grew up."
The winner of the new prize - set to run for an initial three years from 2027 to 2029 - will receive a £2,000 prize and a package of writing support from Fielding's literary agents and New Writing North.
Fielding's original newspaper column went on to be published as a best-selling novel titled Bridget Jones's Diary in 1996.
It spawned several sequels and hit movie adaptations starring Renée Zellweger as the endearingly chaotic and lovelorn thirty-something diarist.
'Comedy heart'
In a statement announcing the prize, external, Fielding noted how the "comedy heart" of Bridget's story came from the "everyday humour of people around me when growing up in Yorkshire: laughing together at our mess-ups; bringing the fancy and pretentious down to earth".

title: Giving £2 a day to people in the Amazon helps protect rainforest, pilot project finds | Amazon rainforest | The Guardian
snippet:
A river snaking through a forest
The experiment involved three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region. Photograph: Martín Mejía/AP
The experiment involved three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region. Photograph: Martín Mejía/AP
Giving £2 a day to people in the Amazon helps protect rainforest, pilot project finds
Researchers say almost 90% of participants in unconditional basic income scheme in Peru adopted environmentally beneficial practices
Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.00 BST
Last modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.02 BST
Share
A pioneering project to provide Indigenous people in the Peruvian Amazon with an unconditional basic income has contributed to the protection of the rainforest, according to a study.
The analysis from the University of Bath is expected to contribute to a growing debate about the role of direct payments to communities that maintain globally important ecosystems.
A two-year pilot managed by the UK-based charity Cool Earth gave 211 people in three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region six cash transfers of 1,032 Peruvian soles each – roughly equivalent to £2 a day – to spend as they wished.
Over the course of the trial, researchers found almost 90% of participants adopted environmentally beneficial practices, such as collective reforestation, restoration of critical water sources and reductions of forest burning.
They also noted a reduction in food insecurity, which can sometimes prompt forest people to start logging or become involved in environmental crimes. Households unable to afford nutritious food fell from 73% to 26%.
Another reported benefit was reduced migration, with the share of participants forced to leave their homes to find work falling from 43% to 18%. Researchers said this allowed more people to remain and protect the forest.
Dr Nick Langridge, a co-author of the report, said: “The findings suggest that when communities have greater security and autonomy, they are better able to protect the ecosystems they depend on.”

title: US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin - BBC News
snippet:
US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin
Stephen Hubbard, an elderly man wearing a light green jumper, sits handcuffed in a glass cubicle in the courtoom.Image source, Reuters
Image caption,
Stephen Hubbard pictured in a Moscow courtroom as he was sentenced in 2024
ByMaia Davies
Published
21 October 2026, 10:22 BST
Updated 24 minutes ago
Russia has released a 74-year-old American citizen who was jailed for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine, as President Vladimir Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg for talks.
Stephen Hubbard has been taken to Pulkovo Airport, Putin said during the meeting early on Wednesday.
President Donald Trump later said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary".
Hubbard was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024. He was accused of serving in a defence unit in Izyum, Ukraine, when he was captured by Russian forces shortly after Moscow's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Writing on social media after Russian state media reported the release, Trump said it had followed a request he "made directly" to Putin last week.
Some other releases of detained Americans from Russia have been obtained through prisoner swaps.
Trump also appeared to defend his recent decision to suspend sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to come into force, writing that "if sanctions would have been placed", negotiations for Hubbard's release "would have come to a complete and total halt".
The US State Department had previously classified Hubbard, from Michigan, as "wrongfully detained" and the US president had suggested on Tuesday that his release may be imminent.
"Watch what happens," Trump told reporters, "we have been focused on Hubbard".
CBS News, the BBC's US media partner, reported that Hubbard had been in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment.

title: Canada v England: Ellie Kildunne on bench as Red Roses ring changes - BBC Sport
snippet:
Kildunne drops to bench as Red Roses ring changes
Ellie Kildunne runs with the ballImage source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Kildunne made more metres (149) and clean breaks (two) and beat more defenders (six) than any other England player in defeat by Canada
By
BBC Sport rugby union news reporter
Published
7 minutes ago
Star full-back Ellie Kildunne has been dropped to the bench as England shake up their selection in response to a first defeat in four years.
Kildunne was part of the starting XV who lost 24-21 to Canada last Friday in Toronto with the Red Roses' unbeaten streak ending at 41 matches.
Head coach John Mitchell has accused his side of losing the hunger that fuelled a run which took in four successive Six Nations Grand Slams and last year's landmark world title on home soil.
"Last Friday, we lost sight of what we could control when it mattered most. That's on us to fix," said Mitchell.
"This week is about getting back to who we are - hungry, accountable to each other and demanding more of ourselves than anyone outside this group ever could."
Figure caption,
Late Canada fightback ends Red Roses' unbeaten streak
Emma Sing comes in at full-back in Kildunne's place for Saturday's rematch (00:00 BST) against Canada in Ottawa, while Tatyana Heard and Claudia Moloney-MacDonald - backline starters in the defeat - drop out of the matchday squad entirely.
Helena Rowland and Mia Venner replace Heard and Moloney-MacDonald at inside centre and wing respectively.
In the fourth change to the starting line-up, Sadia Kabeya, who appeared off the bench last week on her comeback from a leg injury, starts with Alex Matthews, two-time Rugby World Cup winner, dropping to the bench.
Exeter's Flo Robinson and Sale's Hollie Aitchison are included on the bench as a new-look set of half-back replacements.
Sing, a rangy runner who can also kick goals, started two matches at full-back during England's Six Nations campaign, with Kildunne switching to a different position on the wing

snippet:
Watch: Third attempt to save 'celebrity' shark stranded in South Korean canal
Huge crowds have flocked to a canal in South Korea to watch a stranded shark.
The 9ft 10in (3m) shark, nicknamed Bukangi, was first spotted in the waterway last month in the south-eastern city of Busan.
Now a third attempt has been made to rescue the female using nets to guide her back to the open sea.
It is thought the shark may have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm water and plenty of fish.
The BBC's Seoul correspondent Jake Kwon goes to Busan to follow the latest attempt to rescue Bukangi.

ByZoe Conway
Employment correspondent
Published
21 October 2026, 13:08 BST
Updated 31 minutes ago
The civil servant accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by juggling multiple public-sector jobs admitted making mistakes but said ''I do not believe there was criminal intent".
Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court, Kashim Chowdhury told the jury he had made mistakes because he was ''overwhelmed and stressed'' and had felt ''terror and panic'' at the thought of losing his livelihood.
He told the jury he had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder in 2015 and that it had been triggered in 2021.
The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.
The prosecution alleges Chowdhury failed to reveal to his employers that he had other full-time employment. But Chowdhury told the jury some of his managers knew he had other jobs.
His managers at Department for Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra), the London Borough of Tower Hamlets, East London NHS Trust and the Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC) all knew he had other jobs.
The prosecution alleges that at the height of the deceit, Chowdhury held five full-time jobs on full-time salaries within the public sector.
In the spring of 2023, he was employed by Defra, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days.

Hackers steal children's data after company used 'Password1' to protect old account
A close-up of a woman's hand typing on a computer keyboard in the dark against colourful lights in background. The keyboard is lit up.Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Hackers stole information from Data Cymru's systems in 2024 which exposed the personal information of 3,300 people
ByAngharad Thomas
BBC Wales
Published
1 hour ago
A cyber-attack stole information belonging to thousands of children by accessing an account that used the password "Password1", a data watchdog has said.
The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and Data Cymru after the attack on 1 November 2024.
The hackers exposed personal information belonging to 3,300 people, mostly children, by using a test account, known as Test2, which had existed for more than 12 years and was protected by the password that could be compromised in less than a second.
ONL said the account "should have been removed long before criminals were able to use it", adding it had brought in independent cyber-security specialists.
The company, which provided IT services to Data Cymru, said it accepted the ICO's findings and had "acted on them".
Data Cymru merged with the Welsh Local Government Association (WLGA) in 2025, who said there was no evidence the stolen information was "shared further or misused".
ONL and Data Cymru were found to have breached UK GDPR rules, external by failing to properly protect their systems and by not regularly checking whether their security measures were effective.
During the ransomware attack, the hackers encrypted 182.7GB of data and stole 42GB from Data Cymru's systems. It exposed the personal information related to two projects supporting children and families.

9 hours ago
Ana FaguyReporting from East Potomac Golf Links

For Jourdain Yardan, golfing at the East Potomac Golf Links on Washington DC's waterfront is a twice-weekly ritual.
"Anyone from any walk of life, whether they're starting to play golf or whether they're a ... seasoned golfer, they can come out here and play golf at a pretty reasonable rate," the 35-year-old told the BBC while putting on the course on Monday.
But President Donald Trump does not seem convinced of its charms, calling the 106-year-old course "Trash Island" Monday evening on Truth Social.
Now, he intends to shut it down for renovations to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments".
The renovation is part of the president's sprawling and controversial efforts to shape the US capital, which include a new White House ballroom, a 250-foot-tall arch and other changes to longstanding landmarks. The golf course is a smaller project, but deeply personal to many who live in the city.

Trump, an avid golfer and owner of more than a dozen courses, says his vision for the course will make it "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World".

7 hours ago

Bloomberg via Getty Images Stacks of United States Postal Service (USPS) flat tubs sit on a conveyor beltBloomberg via Getty Images
Pakistan's cybercrime agency has arrested a man accused of running a counterfeit operation that caused $126 million (£94m) in losses to the US Postal service.
Faheem Akram is accused of having sold fake stamps via a fraudulent website in the US since 2023.
He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida last month for selling more than five million counterfeit shipping labels to thousands of US customers over the years. Authorities have now shut down the website.
Earlier this month, the US Postal Inspection Service offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest.
According to the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, the 33-year-old from Khanewal, Pakistan, operated LabelsBank.com.
US prosecutors alleged that he sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate regardless of a package's weight, size or destination.
The counterfeit labels, usually sold at $2 each, allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service.
An investigation found that more than 5,200 individuals purchased more than 5.1 million counterfeit shipping labels, the office said in a press release.
Akram is charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels, and four counts of wire fraud.
If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts, and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count, the office said.

Hackers stole information from Data Cymru's systems in 2024 which exposed the personal information of 3,300 people
ByAngharad Thomas
BBC Wales
Published
1 hour ago
A cyber-attack stole information belonging to thousands of children by accessing an account that used the password "Password1", a data watchdog has said.
The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and Data Cymru after the attack on 1 November 2024.
The hackers exposed personal information belonging to 3,300 people, mostly children, by using a test account, known as Test2, which had existed for more than 12 years and was protected by the password that could be compromised in less than a second.
ONL said the account "should have been removed long before criminals were able to use it", adding it had brought in independent cyber-security specialists.
The company, which provided IT services to Data Cymru, said it accepted the ICO's findings and had "acted on them".
Data Cymru merged with the Welsh Local Government Association (WLGA) in 2025, who said there was no evidence the stolen information was "shared further or misused".
ONL and Data Cymru were found to have breached UK GDPR rules, external by failing to properly protect their systems and by not regularly checking whether their security measures were effective.
During the ransomware attack, the hackers encrypted 182.7GB of data and stole 42GB from Data Cymru's systems. It exposed the personal information related to two projects supporting children and families.
David Doodson, head of investigations at the Information Commission's Office, said: "Password1 is not an appropriate password, it is a wide-open door to nefarious actors.

The civil servant accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by juggling multiple public-sector jobs admitted making mistakes but said ''I do not believe there was criminal intent".
Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court, Kashim Chowdhury told the jury he had made mistakes because he was ''overwhelmed and stressed'' and had felt ''terror and panic'' at the thought of losing his livelihood.
He told the jury he had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder in 2015 and that it had been triggered in 2021.
The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.
The prosecution alleges Chowdhury failed to reveal to his employers that he had other full-time employment. But Chowdhury told the jury some of his managers knew he had other jobs.
His managers at Department for Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra), the London Borough of Tower Hamlets, East London NHS Trust and the Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC) all knew he had other jobs.
The prosecution alleges that at the height of the deceit, Chowdhury held five full-time jobs on full-time salaries within the public sector.
In the spring of 2023, he was employed by Defra, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. The International Bureau of Weights and Measures (French: Bureau international des poids et mesures, BIPM) is an intergovernmental organisation (IGO), through which its 67 member-states act on measurement standards in areas such as chemistry, ionising radiation, physical metrology, as well as the International System of Units (SI) and Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).[2][3] It is headquartered in the Pavillon de Breteuil in Saint-Cloud, near Paris, France. The organisation has been referred to as IBWM (from its name in English) in older literature.[note 1]
Function
The BIPM has the mandate to provide the basis for a single, coherent system of measurements throughout the world, traceable to the International System of Units (SI). This task takes many forms, from direct dissemination of units to coordination through international comparisons of national measurement standards (as in electricity and ionising radiation).[5]
Following consultation, a draft version of the BIPM Work Programme is presented at each meeting of the General Conference for consideration with the BIPM budget. The final programme of work is determined by the CIPM in accordance with the budget agreed to by the CGPM.[6][7]

History of the software¶
Python was created in the early 1990s by Guido van Rossum at Stichting Mathematisch Centrum (CWI, see https://www.cwi.nl) in the Netherlands as a successor of a language called ABC. Guido remains Python’s principal author, although it includes many contributions from others.
In 1995, Guido continued his work on Python at the Corporation for National Research Initiatives (CNRI, see https://www.cnri.reston.va.us) in Reston, Virginia where he released several versions of the software.
In May 2000, Guido and the Python core development team moved to BeOpen.com to form the BeOpen PythonLabs team. In October of the same year, the PythonLabs team moved to Digital Creations, which became Zope Corporation. In 2001, the Python Software Foundation (PSF, see https://www.python.org/psf/) was formed, a non-profit organization created specifically to own Python-related Intellectual Property. Zope Corporation was a sponsoring member of the PSF.

Hongwu Emperor
The Hongwu Emperor (21 October 1328 – 24 June 1398), personal name Zhu Yuanzhang, was the founding emperor of the Ming dynasty of China, reigning from 1368 to 1398. Born into a peasant family in Anhui, Zhu grew up amid famine, epidemics, and unrest under the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty. Orphaned at 16, he briefly lived as a novice monk before joining the Red Turban rebels in 1352. Rising rapidly, he captured Nanjing in 1356, established a regional regime, and defeated rival rebels. In 1368, he proclaimed the Ming dynasty, adopted the era name Hongwu, and expelled the Yuan from China proper. During his 30-year reign, he restored stability after decades of war, strengthened state institutions, promoted agriculture, and maintained a disciplined army while seeking to limit civilian suffering. He died in 1398 and was succeeded by his grandson, the Jianwen Emperor, who was overthrown in 1402 by Zhu Di, later known as the Yongle Emperor. (Full article...)

All links on the BBC Public Service site or on the editorial pages of a BBC Commercial site must be editorially justifiable

The producer must check the contents of the external site before adding a link to a BBC page.
BBC sites which cover matters of controversy or public policy may offer links to external sites which, taken together, represent a reasonable range of views about the subject.
For programme support pages, an external link should be justified by the relevance and value of the material to the programme's audience.
When linking to any commercial site, great care must be taken to avoid giving the impression that the BBC is endorsing a commercial product or service.

title: Aberfan marks 60 years since coal tip collapsed on school and homes, killing 116 children and 28 adults - BBC News
snippet:
Summary
People in Aberfan, south Wales, are remembering the disaster 60 years ago when a coal waste tip collapsed on a school and homes
On 21 October 1966, 116 children and 28 adults were killed when the colliery spoil tip collapsed and engulfed Pantglas Junior School and surrounding houses
Emergency services, miners and people who rushed to the village began an around-the-clock battle to dig out those trapped by the debris
Mair Morgan, the last surviving teacher at the school, still remembers having to identify the children who died
King Charles, Queen Camilla and the Prince of Wales are joining survivors, bereaved parents and other members of the community at a memorial garden that stands on the site of the school
A prayer and moment of silence was held at 09:15 to mark the moment the coal spoil struck the village
Warning: This live page will contain upsetting details that some may find distressing

They will meet survivors, bereaved parents and members of the community to pay tribute to the 144 people who lost their lives.

Christina Applegate thought she was living with multiple sclerosis (MS) for five years, until recently discovering she had been given a wrong diagnosis.
The actress, known for hits like Anchorman and Married With Children, said she was "not happy at all" about the news and in tears when she found out.
"You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said in an episode of her Messy podcast released on Tuesday. "If anything, I've gotten worse."
The two-part episode, co-hosted by Jamie Sigler, ends a recent break she took to process the information. An investigation into what has been causing her debilitating symptoms - which she experiences daily - will begin next week.
"I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me," she said.
In the podcast, Applegate said that "all of a sudden, a few years ago", her doctor suggested ending her infusion treatment for MS to see how her body reacted.
During the time off, her body did not respond in a way that would indicate she had MS.
Doctors then looked into her case further and concluded she did not have the autoimmune disease, which can cause muscle stiffness and problems with walking and talking.
"She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,' " Applegate said, recalling the moment.
"I was, like, not happy at all," she continued. "Everybody else was so happy."
Misdiagnoses can be extremely distressing for people dealing with chronic illnesses, said Dr Michael Kornberg.
"It becomes part of your identity," the associate professor of neurology at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine said, noting how there is a "comfort" in knowing what is happening inside your body.
"To live with that for five years and then to be given a different diagnosis is really unsettling."

The BBC has a long tradition of making information available and accessible. It seeks to be open and accountable and already provides the public with a great deal of information about its activities. BBC accessibility policy
In keeping with its public service remit, and its obligations under the Disability Discrimination Act, the BBC will ensure that its media is accessible to people who have visual, hearing, motor or cognitive impairments.
Accessibility is a partnership between site producers like the BBC and the creators of the operating system, browser, and specialist assistive technologies which many disabled users employ to allow them, for example, to view websites in easier-to-read colours, with larger fonts, or as spoken text.
As such technologies have become more available and sophisticated, the BBC will:
Ensure that its media work well with these assistive technologies to ensure an accessible experience for disabled users.

Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda
Associated Press
Wed 21 Oct 2026 01.14 BST

Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.
The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.
The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.
Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.
“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”.

Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs
Kashim Chowdhury wears dark sunglasses, a hat, hoody and gloves as he arrives at court. His face is largely obscured.Image source, PA Media
Image caption,
Civil servant Kashim Chowdhury is accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by working multiple full-time public sector jobs
ByZoe Conway
Employment correspondent
Published
21 October 2026, 13:08 BST
Updated 34 minutes ago
The civil servant accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by juggling multiple public-sector jobs admitted making mistakes but said ''I do not believe there was criminal intent".
Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court, Kashim Chowdhury told the jury he had made mistakes because he was ''overwhelmed and stressed'' and had felt ''terror and panic'' at the thought of losing his livelihood.
He told the jury he had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder in 2015 and that it had been triggered in 2021.
The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.
The prosecution alleges Chowdhury failed to reveal to his employers that he had other full-time employment. But Chowdhury told the jury some of his managers knew he had other jobs.
His managers at Department for Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra), the London Borough of Tower Hamlets, East London NHS Trust and the Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC) all knew he had other jobs.
The prosecution alleges that at the height of the deceit, Chowdhury held five full-time jobs on full-time salaries within the public sector.
In the spring of 2023, he was employed by Defra, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days.

A teenage boy who had a hatred of women and an "obsessive interest" in killers has been found guilty of the attempted murder of a girl at his school.
The boy dressed in black and wore a face mask before stabbing the 15-year-old victim in the back at Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, in March.
Armed police were called to the school, which went into lockdown, and the attack was caught on CCTV.
The boy, who is 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, wrote notes about hating women and had an "obsessive and dangerous interest in killers and killing", jurors at King's Lynn Crown Court were told. He will be sentenced on 18 December.
Jurors deliberated for just under four hours before delivering a majority verdict at the end of a trial which began two weeks ago.
The teenager "went to school not to learn, but to kill" while armed with a kitchen knife, the prosecution said.
The school went into lockdown after the attack and there was an armed police response, while the girl was taken to hospital with a minor injury.

Few events have left a deeper mark on Wales than the Aberfan disaster.
Sixty years on, the tragedy remains woven into the nation's collective memory, a day of unimaginable loss that reshaped a community and changed attitudes to industrial safety across Britain.
At 09:15 on 21 October 1966, an ordinary school morning was shattered when a coal tip above Aberfan collapsed.

title: Formula 1: Races to return to standard distance in 2028 - BBC Sport
snippet:
F1 races to return to standard distance in 2028
Formula 1 cars at the 2026 Azerbaijan Grand PrixImage source, Getty Images
Image caption,
The maximum distance of a Formula 1 race will be reduced by 15km in 2027
By
F1 correspondent
Published
1 hour ago
Formula 1 grands prix will return to their standard distance in 2028 after the maximum length was shortened for next season.
The maximum distance of a race was cut by 15km from 305km (189.5 miles) to 290km (180.2 miles) for the 2027 season.
That reduction was introduced because of a quirk of the situation surrounding changes to the engine rules for next year.
The new hybrid engines introduced this year, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, have been criticised for reducing the impact of driver skill.
The power split will be changed, in two steps, to 60-40 by 2028, enabling drivers to have maximum power for longer.
This means the cars will use more fuel - and that became a concern when it emerged some teams wanted to carry their chassis over into next year to save money.
As the fuel tank is within the chassis and therefore its size could not be changed, this meant those teams might not have been able to finish grands prix with their existing fuel tanks.
The change affects only a handful of races where fuel consumption is heaviest.
The sport's governing body, the FIA, published the 2027 rules this week and these included a section on changes for 2028 in which there is a clause that removes the reduction and reinstates the 305km maximum distance.
Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton had previously objected to the shortening of race distances.
Britain's Hamilton, 41, said: "The races should be longer because the races are physically easier than ever before. So shortening, I don't think, makes much sense.

title: Missing German WW2 U-boat discovered off Devon 82 years on - BBC News
snippet:
Missing German WW2 U-boat found 82 years on
An underwater view of a submarine wreck, with fish swimming around it.Image source, Gasperados
Image caption,
The U-boat was scuttled by its own crew after it was attacked by the Royal Navy in July 1944
ByJohnny Rutherford and Britta ZeltmannDevon
Published
7 hours ago
A German submarine that went missing during World War Two after being damaged by the Royal Navy has been discovered 82 years on.
Plymouth dive team Gasperados identified the U-672 about 20 miles (32km) off Salcombe, Devon, after it was discovered by a deep sea diving team from Portland in August at a depth of about 230ft (70m).
The vessel was attacked by HMS Balfour in July 1944 but was scuttled by its 52 crew - all of whom survived. A navy log showing the sinking had incorrect coordinates, resulting in it not being found until recently.
Members of Gasperados said they were "really pleased" they could help identify the vessel.
Gasperados diver Dominic Robinson said: "Once we started moving around it and I started seeing the individual features - I saw the snorkel, I saw the conning tower, all those kind of things - I knew that we were going to get the video needed to identify it, so I was really pleased about that."
After its attack, the U-boat was left leaking underwater.
Its commander waited for as long as possible before making the decision to blow the tanks and bring the sub up to give its crew a last chance of survival.
Robinson said they "managed to get it to the surface" before getting into their life rafts for survival.
"They were bobbing around in the sea and then the very next day they were found by British aircraft, British vessels and then taken away to the prisoner of war camp," he explained.

snippet:
Where to spot brilliant colours after 'false autumn' spoils some leaf displays
An aerial photo shows a single carriageway road on which a white car is driving, cutting through a forest which has trees with a variety of redm orange and gree coloured leaves.Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
There was a stunning display of autumnal colours in 2025 after a warm and sunny summer, but how will this year's heat affect the seasonal display?
Published
21 October 2026, 00:04 BST
This year's display of autumn leaves could look rather different following the UK's hottest summer on record.
Months of heat and drought have put trees under stress, causing some to shed their leaves earlier than usual in a phenomenon known as a "false autumn".
Experts say this could mean a more varied display of autumn colours, with some trees losing their leaves prematurely while others are yet to change colour.
However, some trees could still produce spectacular shades of red, orange and gold.
How has the hot summer affected trees?
The UK's record-breaking summer brought prolonged periods of heat and dry weather, with some parts of the country particularly affected by drought.
Kevin Martin, Head of Tree Collections at Royal Bontanic Gardens, Kew, said: "Following the UK's hottest summer on record, we may not see the usual blaze of autumn colour arrive all at once this year."
Many trees, particularly in southern England, have already shed their leaves prematurely. This happens when trees respond to heat and drought stress by dropping their leaves early to conserve water.
"False autumns are a warning sign. Trees can live for hundreds of years, but they are increasingly under pressure from a rapidly changing climate," Martin said.
However, some trees could still produce spectacular autumn colours.

History of the software¶
Python was created in the early 1990s by Guido van Rossum at Stichting Mathematisch Centrum (CWI, see https://www.cwi.nl) in the Netherlands as a successor of a language called ABC. Guido remains Python’s principal author, although it includes many contributions from others.
In 1995, Guido continued his work on Python at the Corporation for National Research Initiatives (CNRI, see https://www.cnri.reston.va.us) in Reston, Virginia where he released several versions of the software.
In May 2000, Guido and the Python core development team moved to BeOpen.com to form the BeOpen PythonLabs team. In October of the same year, the PythonLabs team moved to Digital Creations, which became Zope Corporation. In 2001, the Python Software Foundation (PSF, see https://www.python.org/psf/) was formed, a non-profit organization created specifically to own Python-related Intellectual Property. Zope Corporation was a sponsoring member of the PSF.

The Ming dynasty was founded by the peasant rebel leader Zhu Yuanzhang, known as the Hongwu Emperor. All Ming emperors were of the House of Zhu. title: Tesla and SpaceX: Why does Elon Musk want to merge the companies?
snippet:
Why is Elon Musk plotting a mega-merger of SpaceX and Tesla?
6 hours ago
Osmond ChiaBusiness reporter
Getty Images/Reuters A composite picture shows Elon Musk wearing a blue suit jacket and white shirt next to a photo of a Tesla car and a picture of a SpaceX rocket taking offGetty Images/Reuters
Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together.
Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."
The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.
With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.
Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.
How likely is the merger?

The emperors of the Ming dynasty ruled over China proper from 1368 to 1644 during the late imperial era of China (960–1912). Members of the Ming dynasty continued to rule a series of rump states in southern China, commonly known as the Southern Ming, until 1662; the Ming dynasty succeeded the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty and preceded the Manchu-led Qing dynasty.
The Ming dynasty was founded by the peasant rebel leader Zhu Yuanzhang, known as the Hongwu Emperor. All Ming emperors were of the House of Zhu. The longest-reigning emperor of the dynasty was the Wanli Emperor (r. 1572–1620), who ruled for 48 years; the shortest was his successor, the Taichang Emperor, who ruled for only 29 days in 1620. The Cross, also known as The Barre Cross, God's Wisdom, or The Ten Commandments on Earth, is a large privately created geoglyph park in Barre, Massachusetts, United States. John P. Harty Sr. started the project in 1989 and it opened to the public in 1992. Main features include a large asphalt cross on the ground with the Ten Commandments written on it, trees spelling out the text "God's Wisdom", and a holy well.
Inspiration
Tool dealer John P. Harty Sr. said that at the age of 67 when he was saying the Lord's Prayer laying in his bed around midnight on March 16, 1989, he heard a clear voice from God giving him a set of instructions to create a large monument including the Ten Commandments and "Love thy neighbor as thyself" written on a cross on his farmland.[1] Harty claimed that through a series of visions, he learned several details about what to create, including a pond, a well, a message made of trees, and dimensions for the construction.[2] After completing the main project in 1992, Harty opened it to the public saying that he expected many people would soon come to see his cross.[1]

Public School 109 (P.S. 109), also known as El Barrio's Artspace PS109, is a school building at 215 East 99th Street in the East Harlem neighborhood of Manhattan, New York City, United States. Designed by Charles B. J. Snyder, it is five stories high. The building has an H-shaped floor plan with wings flanking a pair of courtyards. The base of the building is clad in limestone, and the first through fifth stories have brick facades with terracotta decoration. The building has a steel superstructure and initially included simple classroom spaces, which have since been converted into 90 apartments.
The P.S. 109 building was constructed between 1898 and 1909 to replace an earlier school in a tobacco factory. The building operated as a public school until 1996, when severe deterioration prompted a sudden evacuation. P.S. 109 was closed and nearly demolished, but it was saved due to opposition from preservationists. Following an extended period of abandonment, it was converted into a cultural and housing complex for artists. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and is a New York City designated landmark.

reporting from Ohio
Published
21 October 2026, 03:37 BST
In this closely fought midterm election campaign, the small town of Springfield, Ohio, has become a symbol of modern America. But it is a symbol that changes dramatically depending on who is describing it.
To President Donald Trump, Springfield crystallises America's problems due to years of unchecked immigration. He once echoed a false claim that Haitian immigrants were eating pets here. Today, he says his mass deportation drive means its people are "getting their town back".
But to others, Springfield represents a well-known cycle in the story of modern America. The decline of traditional industry, followed by a spike in immigration fuelled by cheap housing and low-paid labour. It is a familiar tale across the country.
This story contains some distressing details
Pierre Damas Bel, 20, arrived in Springfield to join his father and stepmother in 2024.
He fled his native Haiti, which was gripped by political instability and gang warfare. He entered the US with the government's permission under a now-defunct Biden-era programme for migrants waiting in Mexico.
Bel, according to a family friend, then received a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which gives vetted individuals the right to live and work in the United States.
TPS usually lasts 18 months but is routinely rolled over, often for years, if the danger remains in the affected country.

title: Is Donald Trump ready to do business with Myanmar?
snippet:
Is Donald Trump ready to do business with Myanmar?
13 hours ago
Jonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondent
Getty Images Min Aung HlaingGetty Images
A top US official recently met with Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing for the first time in years
Has Washington's long-standing policy of isolating the military regime in Myanmar now changed?
The revelation that a top official in the Trump administration met its leader Min Aung Hlaing last month, and the removal of some business figures from the US sanctions list, suggests that it has.
Until now, the US had had very little official contact with the regime following the 2021 coup, when Myanmar's military ousted democratically-elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi. More recently, it had applied a series of targeted sanctions against those judged to be supporting the junta.
The meeting on 15 and 16 September was with US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance, and it took place in Myanmar's capital Nay Pyi Taw. Its ostensible focus was to secure the release of Adam Castillo, a US citizen who had been detained in June over a dispute with the local American Chamber of Commerce.
But Vance was the most senior US official to meet Min Aung Hlaing since he seized power, and they almost certainly discussed other matters of mutual interest.
Vance is also known to have met Burmese officials in Tokyo in June, again in Tokyo this month, and to have met representatives of the groups opposing military rule.
Signs of a shift in US policy towards Myanmar, though, go back to July last year, at the height of President Donald Trump's tariff war.
That was when Min Aung Hlaing, along with other leaders in the region, received a personal letter from the US president informing him that his country's shattered economy was about to be hit by, in Myanmar's case, 40% tariffs.
Other countries reeled in shock at the punitive levies imposed on their vital trade with a country they had once seen as a friend and ally.

title: BBC closures make business sense, but far more savings are needed, says Katie Razzall
snippet:
Katie Razzall: BBC closures make business sense, but far more savings are needed
22 hours ago
Katie RazzallCulture and media editor
Getty Images The BBC logo is seen displayed on a smartphone screenGetty Images
The BBC's announcement that it will close three of its linear broadcast channels - BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra - makes sense financially.
BBC Three's most popular show on Monday night was a repeat of an old episode of Top Gear. Around 77,000 people tuned in.
BBC Scotland's TV channel was watched, according to this year's annual report, by a weekly average of 12% of the Scottish population. Scots simply aren't tuning in in the numbers to make it cost-effective.
(Interestingly, BBC Alba, which is aimed at Gaelic speakers and learners, reached 43% of Gaelic viewers in Scotland weekly - was it boosted by its rights to broadcast Italian football's Serie A?)
It's hard to argue - although no doubt some will - that there is a business case for keeping BBC Scotland's TV channel open.
The same goes for BBC Three, although the hokey cokey that has gone on with that channel - launched to fanfare in 2003, later made digital-only, then brought back to linear in 2022, now back online only again - has looked indecisive. Bizarre even.
But the bigger picture is that viewers and listeners are already migrating online - increasingly finding the BBC's programmes not via those linear TV and radio channels but on iPlayer, BBC Sounds, and, more recently, YouTube.
So that's the business case - and the BBC needs to save £500m over the next three years. That figure is concentrating minds.
But axing the three linear channels is a drop in the ocean financially. I understand it will save less than £10m in total per year.

The Met Office has issued an amber weather warning for strong winds as Storm Austen is forecast to sweep across parts of the UK.
The warning - the second-highest tier that the Met Office issues - is valid for Cornwall and parts of west Devon from 03:00 until 10:00 BST on Friday.
Wind gusts of up to 80mph (130km/h) are expected around exposed coasts, with 60-70mph gusts elsewhere.
Flying debris could lead to injuries or a danger to life, with the risk of power cuts and damage to buildings.
A broader yellow Met Office wind warning covers large swathes of southern England and south Wales with some travel disruption possible.
Southern and eastern Scotland is also covered by a Met Office yellow warning - this one for heavy rain which could bring the risk of flooding.

Storm Austen - an area of low pressure - is currently developing in the Atlantic and will continue to deepen as it approaches the UK.
It will move close to south-west England on Thursday night with the strongest winds expected to arrive early on Friday morning.
The very windiest conditions are expected on coastal headlands in north and west Cornwall - exposed to the north-westerly gales - but gusts of up to 70mph could occur even in inland areas.

Controversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) secretary, had their offices in Guinea-Bissau raided by judicial police, who seized doses of hepatitis B vaccines, officials said on Facebook.
The researchers have been at the heart of an ongoing dispute over research on African newborns, supported by $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and matched by the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation for a total of $3.2m.
The police search took place on Monday, involving “investigative procedures aimed at clarifying the circumstances related to the said batch of vaccines”, according to the social media post, which was translated from Portuguese. The announcement noted that seizing the immunizations did not point to “irregularities in the quality, safety, or effectiveness of the vaccines”.
The Bandim Health Project recently posted a letter of approval for the trial from Guinea-Bissau’s national ethics committee at the ministry of public health, dated 14 July and signed by the committee’s president, Mouhammed Djicó Ould Ahmed. A Danish research ethics committee, which had to change its rules to consider a clinical trial, also approved the study earlier this month.

Mon 19 Oct 2026 10.08 BST
Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 16.36 BST

There is mounting concern over the safety of Japan’s traditional festivals after the death of a senior local official who was reportedly crushed beneath a float at the weekend, days after two men died in similar incidents in another part of the country.
Akihiro Nabae, the deputy mayor of Saijo, in western Japan, was carrying a giant float with other participants in a festival on Saturday when he became trapped beneath the structure, Agence France-Presse reported. Nabae, 62, was taken to hospital and later pronounced dead, local media said, adding that no one else was injured.
He died less than two weeks after a 51-year-old man was crushed beneath a wooden float he was riding at one of the annual Danjiri festivals held in southern Osaka prefecture. The same day, a 48-year-old man was killed in a similar accident at a Danjiri event in a nearby town. Police said 16 people were injured in the incidents.

title: ctypes — A foreign function library for Python — Python 3.15.0 documentation
snippet:
ctypes — A foreign function library for Python¶
Source code: Lib/ctypes
ctypes is a foreign function library for Python. It provides C compatible data types, and allows calling functions in DLLs or shared libraries. It can be used to wrap these libraries in pure Python.
This is an optional module. If it is missing from your copy of CPython, look for documentation from your distributor (that is, whoever provided Python to you). If you are the distributor, see Requirements for optional modules.
Warning
ctypes provides low-level access to native libraries and the process’s memory, bypassing Python’s safety mechanisms and allowing execution of arbitrary native code. Incorrect use can corrupt data and objects, reveal sensitive information, cause crashes, or otherwise compromise the running process.
ctypes tutorial¶
Note: Some code samples reference the ctypes c_int type. On platforms where sizeof(long) == sizeof(int) it is an alias to c_long. So, you should not be confused if c_long is printed if you would expect c_int — they are actually the same type.
Loading dynamic link libraries¶
ctypes exports the cdll, and on Windows windll and oledll objects, for loading dynamic link libraries.
You load libraries by accessing them as attributes of these objects. cdll loads libraries which export functions using the standard cdecl calling convention, while windll libraries call functions using the stdcall calling convention. oledll also uses the stdcall calling convention, and assumes the functions return a Windows HRESULT error code. The error code is used to automatically raise an OSError exception when the function call fails.
Changed in version 3.3: Windows errors used to raise WindowsError, which is now an alias of OSError.
Here are some examples for Windows. Note that msvcrt is the MS standard C library containing most standard C functions, and uses the cdecl calling convention:

Some of these modules are explicitly designed to encourage and enhance the portability of Python programs by abstracting away platform-specifics into platform-neutral APIs.
The Python installers for the Windows platform usually include the entire standard library and often also include many additional components. For Unix-like operating systems Python is normally provided as a collection of packages, so it may be necessary to use the packaging tools provided with the operating system to obtain some or all of the optional components.

urllib.request — Extensible library for opening URLs¶
The urllib.request module defines functions and classes which help in opening URLs (mostly HTTP) in a complex world — basic and digest authentication, redirections, cookies and more.

She was harassed for crude remarks about Modi at a Cockroach protest. Now she can’t leave home
After a protest clip went viral, a teenager’s life was torn apart by threats that sent her and her family into hiding. Plus, a book on citizen journalism
Niha Masih
Tue 20 Oct 2026 07.30 BST
Last modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.50 BST

Before 24 July, a person I will call R was preoccupied with the ordinary routines of teenage life: experimenting with makeup, grumbling over mathematics homework and hanging out with friends at a tea stall.
That month, as the fever of student protests spread across the country, the 15-year-old watched on her phone as young people poured into Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, demanding education reform. She went too. But an 11-second video clip from the protest site, in which she made crude and profane remarks about the prime minister, Narendra Modi, upended her life.
“I feel like a criminal, as if I murdered someone,” R said in her first interview about life since the backlash. “I didn’t get a chance to make amends. In my own country, I am being treated like an enemy.”
It’s been 86 days since that protest, but R doesn’t leave home over safety concerns, trapped in the reality the ordeal created.
The summer agitation had for weeks demanded the ousting of the then-education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, over repeated examination paper leaks. But after a violent police crackdown on a student march the anger spilled over to the Modi government.

title: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism
snippet:
Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite new optimism
17 hours ago
Paul AdamsDiplomatic correspondent
EPA (L-R) Finnish President Alexander Stubb, US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store meet in Oslo. Zelensky and Witkoff are hugging.EPA
Witkoff and Zelensky met in the Norwegian capital
The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky before talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.
Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"
But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?
The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all?
Both in rhetoric and actions, the past 10 days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.
Just listen to the way they talk about each other.
"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.
The verbal assault has continued this week.
"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.
Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.
In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, using an expletive while criticising Benjamin Netanyahu's judgement. Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".
"Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."

"Our commitment to impartiality is at the heart of that relationship of trust. In all our output we will treat every subject with an impartiality that reflects the full range of views. We will consider all the relevant facts fairly and with an open mind."

title: BBC closures make business sense, but far more savings are needed, says Katie Razzall
snippet:
Katie Razzall: BBC closures make business sense, but far more savings are needed
22 hours ago
Katie RazzallCulture and media editor
Getty Images The BBC logo is seen displayed on a smartphone screenGetty Images
The BBC's announcement that it will close three of its linear broadcast channels - BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra - makes sense financially.
BBC Three's most popular show on Monday night was a repeat of an old episode of Top Gear. Around 77,000 people tuned in.
BBC Scotland's TV channel was watched, according to this year's annual report, by a weekly average of 12% of the Scottish population. Scots simply aren't tuning in in the numbers to make it cost-effective.
(Interestingly, BBC Alba, which is aimed at Gaelic speakers and learners, reached 43% of Gaelic viewers in Scotland weekly - was it boosted by its rights to broadcast Italian football's Serie A?)
It's hard to argue - although no doubt some will - that there is a business case for keeping BBC Scotland's TV channel open.
The same goes for BBC Three, although the hokey cokey that has gone on with that channel - launched to fanfare in 2003, later made digital-only, then brought back to linear in 2022, now back online only again - has looked indecisive. Bizarre even.
But the bigger picture is that viewers and listeners are already migrating online - increasingly finding the BBC's programmes not via those linear TV and radio channels but on iPlayer, BBC Sounds, and, more recently, YouTube.
So that's the business case - and the BBC needs to save £500m over the next three years. That figure is concentrating minds.
But axing the three linear channels is a drop in the ocean financially. I understand it will save less than £10m in total per year.

Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.
The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.
The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.
Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.
“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”.

The Hongwu Emperor (21 October 1328 – 24 June 1398), personal name Zhu Yuanzhang, was the founding emperor of the Ming dynasty of China, reigning from 1368 to 1398. Born into a peasant family in Anhui, Zhu grew up amid famine, epidemics, and unrest under the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty. Orphaned at 16, he briefly lived as a novice monk before joining the Red Turban rebels in 1352. Rising rapidly, he captured Nanjing in 1356, established a regional regime, and defeated rival rebels. In 1368, he proclaimed the Ming dynasty, adopted the era name Hongwu, and expelled the Yuan from China proper. During his 30-year reign, he restored stability after decades of war, strengthened state institutions, promoted agriculture, and maintained a disciplined army while seeking to limit civilian suffering. He died in 1398 and was succeeded by his grandson, the Jianwen Emperor, who was overthrown in 1402 by Zhu Di, later known as the Yongle Emperor. (Full article...)

snippet:
Author Helen Fielding launches award to find the next Bridget Jones's Diary
Renée Zellweger (left) and Helen Fielding pictured together while attending the Bridget Jones Scenes in the Square statue unveiling at Leicester Square, London in 2025Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding (right) alongside film star Renée Zellweger
ByPaul Glynn
Culture reporter
Published
2 hours ago
Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding has launched a new prize aimed at discovering funny diary writers from the north of England, saying opportunities across the UK are "very uneven".
West Yorkshire-born Fielding, who penned Bridget's famous diary as well co-writing the film adaptations, has set up the Bridget Jones Prize, external with charity New Writing North.
The award will go to the person who submits the funniest 1,000-word piece of first-person writing.
Speaking at an event for the Independent, which first published Bridget's diary in 1995, Fielding said the spread of opportunity for writing in the UK is "very uneven", adding: "There's much more opportunity in the south than in the north, where I grew up."
The winner of the new prize - set to run for an initial three years from 2027 to 2029 - will receive a £2,000 prize and a package of writing support from Fielding's literary agents and New Writing North.
Fielding's original newspaper column went on to be published as a best-selling novel titled Bridget Jones's Diary in 1996.
It spawned several sequels and hit movie adaptations starring Renée Zellweger as the endearingly chaotic and lovelorn thirty-something diarist.
'Comedy heart'
In a statement announcing the prize, external, Fielding noted how the "comedy heart" of Bridget's story came from the "everyday humour of people around me when growing up in Yorkshire: laughing together at our mess-ups; bringing the fancy and pretentious down to earth".

snippet:
Data-breach NHS worker told woman she had cancer
A woman in a brown cardigan and a silk scarf is looking intently into the camera with her hands clasped together. She is standing in front of green fields.
Image caption,
Pippa Boardman was told she had cancer by a hospital worker, days before her scheduled appointment with a consultant
By
South West health correspondent
Published
7 hours ago
A woman was told she had cancer by a hospital employee who accessed her record days before she was due to receive test results from her consultant.
Pippa Boardman, from Lostwithiel in Cornwall, said she had lost her dignity and privacy through the data breach at the Royal Cornwall Hospital in Truro. She said she did not receive an apology from the hospital until it was contacted by the BBC.
The trust said it was "truly sorry" and "appropriate action had been taken".
It added: "While we cannot disclose the details of individual employment matters, we want to reassure Ms Boardman that we have treated this extremely seriously."
Boardman, who is now recovering well from cancer, said her personal information was accessed by a man she vaguely knew who worked at the hospital.
She said: "I got a phone call at home from somebody I know through the sport that I play.
"This man said to me 'Pippa, I don't want you to worry, but you've got cancer'.
"I just couldn't really believe it".
Two days later Boardman was told by her consultant she did have breast cancer.
Nine months on, she said her strong recovery did not undo the damage done by the experience, adding: "I lost my dignity and I've lost my privacy."
Along with Boardman's case there have also been other recent NHS data breaches, described by Health Secretary Yvette Cooper as a disgrace.

Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates were stabbed to death by Valdo Calocane
ByIsaac Ashe
East Midlands
Published
17 October 2026
Further members of staff have been sacked by an NHS trust for inappropriately accessing medical records of the Nottingham attacks victims.
Nottingham students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, who was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.
In May, Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust confirmed it had dismissed 11 members of staff and, in an update on Friday, said a total of 15 people had now been sacked as part of its investigation.
Dr Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's father, said: "I am appalled, it's time to get a handle on these failures."
He added: "Clearly, the way that the highest confidential data, which is medical data, is being looked at by voyeuristic people in the NHS is disgraceful."
Dr Manjeet Shehmar, medical director at NUH, said: "There is simply no excuse for accessing the records of a patient without a legitimate reason and I hope this sends a really clear message - we will investigate and we will take action.
"To lose a loved one in the way that the families of Ian, Grace and Barnaby have is heartbreaking enough.
"I am so sorry that they have had this further compounded by the actions of these staff members."

Hongwu Emperor
The Hongwu Emperor (21 October 1328 – 24 June 1398), personal name Zhu Yuanzhang, was the founding emperor of the Ming dynasty of China, reigning from 1368 to 1398. Born into a peasant family in Anhui, Zhu grew up amid famine, epidemics, and unrest under the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty. Orphaned at 16, he briefly lived as a novice monk before joining the Red Turban rebels in 1352. Rising rapidly, he captured Nanjing in 1356, established a regional regime, and defeated rival rebels. In 1368, he proclaimed the Ming dynasty, adopted the era name Hongwu, and expelled the Yuan from China proper. During his 30-year reign, he restored stability after decades of war, strengthened state institutions, promoted agriculture, and maintained a disciplined army while seeking to limit civilian suffering. He died in 1398 and was succeeded by his grandson, the Jianwen Emperor, who was overthrown in 1402 by Zhu Di, later known as the Yongle Emperor. (Full article...)

In 1368, he proclaimed the Ming dynasty, adopted the era name Hongwu, and expelled the Yuan from China proper. During his 30-year reign, he restored stability after decades of war, strengthened state institutions, promoted agriculture, and maintained a disciplined army while seeking to limit civilian suffering. Watch: Third attempt to save 'celebrity' shark stranded in South Korean canal
Huge crowds have flocked to a canal in South Korea to watch a stranded shark.
The 9ft 10in (3m) shark, nicknamed Bukangi, was first spotted in the waterway last month in the south-eastern city of Busan.
Now a third attempt has been made to rescue the female using nets to guide her back to the open sea.
It is thought the shark may have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm water and plenty of fish.
The BBC's Seoul correspondent Jake Kwon goes to Busan to follow the latest attempt to rescue Bukangi.

Access services at the BBC
The BBC is funded by and established to serve, all licence fee payers. That means producing public service content that appeals to the breadth of the UK public, and distributing programmes and services in a way which makes them accessible to the maximum number of licence fee payers.
Contents
Subtitles
Audio description
Signing
Throughout its history, the BBC has pioneered technological innovation. From early experiments with closed subtitling and audio description to the breakthrough technology of the K-LIVE re-speaking live subtitling system, the BBC’s R&D teams have lead the field in finding ways to make the BBC’s content more accessible to audiences with special needs.
The BBC is regulated in its delivery of Access Services by Ofcom and we follow their Code on Television Access Service. We report on our performance in the BBC Annual report, and you can see how our delivery compares with other broadcasters in Ofcom’s annual Access Services Reports.
The BBC is currently supported in its delivery of Access Services for its public service television channels by Ericsson Broadcast and Media Services.
Access services at the BBC
Subtitles
Subtitles provide a transcript of the television soundtrack, helping deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers to follow programmes.
Since 2008 the BBC has provided subtitles on 100% of its programme content broadcast on BBC One, BBC Two - including national and regional variants - BBC Four, BBC News, CBBC and CBeebies and continues to provide subtitles on 100% of BBC Three online long-form programming.
BBC technologists have played a key role in developing the technical standards for subtitling over many years. In 1979, a documentary about deaf children called Quietly In Switzerland became the first BBC programme to carry subtitles using the brand new Ceefax technology.
