snippet:
Hackers steal children's data after company used 'Password1' to protect old account
A close-up of a woman's hand typing on a computer keyboard in the dark against colourful lights in background. The keyboard is lit up.Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Hackers stole information from Data Cymru's systems in 2024 which exposed the personal information of 3,300 people
ByAngharad Thomas
BBC Wales
Published
1 hour ago
A cyber-attack stole information belonging to thousands of children by accessing an account that used the password "Password1", a data watchdog has said.
The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and Data Cymru after the attack on 1 November 2024.
The hackers exposed personal information belonging to 3,300 people, mostly children, by using a test account, known as Test2, which had existed for more than 12 years and was protected by the password that could be compromised in less than a second.
ONL said the account "should have been removed long before criminals were able to use it", adding it had brought in independent cyber-security specialists.
The company, which provided IT services to Data Cymru, said it accepted the ICO's findings and had "acted on them".
Data Cymru merged with the Welsh Local Government Association (WLGA) in 2025, who said there was no evidence the stolen information was "shared further or misused".
ONL and Data Cymru were found to have breached UK GDPR rules, external by failing to properly protect their systems and by not regularly checking whether their security measures were effective.
During the ransomware attack, the hackers encrypted 182.7GB of data and stole 42GB from Data Cymru's systems. It exposed the personal information related to two projects supporting children and families.
David Doodson, head of investigations at the Information Commission's Office, said: "Password1 is not an appropriate password, it is a wide-open door to nefarious actors.

Richard Jackson with a beard and short hair wearing a navy blue hoodie with you are enough written on it in white. He has a neutral expression and there is a fence and foilage behind him.Image source, Maddie Birch-Jackson
Image caption,
Former civil servant Richard Jackson made headlines in 2008 when he left top secret files on a train
ByJennifer Meierhans
Published
21 October 2026, 00:05 BST
Warning: This story contains a reference to suicide
It was an ordinary Tuesday train ride to work when top civil servant Richard Jackson made the biggest mistake of his life. By the time he realised, with a sudden jolt of panic, it was too late.
He had left highly classified documents on the train.
The split-second error became national news and Jackson's life was thrown into turmoil. He was consumed by shame and humiliation.
Nearly 20 years on, he recounts that fateful day and the aftermath, speaking to Dr Sian Williams for BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast. He says he is proof that even when you've made your worst mistake you can rebuild your life.
Before his life unravelled, Jackson was 37 and living in Yateley in Hampshire with wife Maddie and stepdaughter Charlotte, 15. His other stepdaughter Becky, 20, was at university.
"We were very happy," he says. "But I was very focused on my career.
"My worth and my value came from that career, job title, position and responsibility.
"I found myself working 100-hour weeks for a while," he says. "I didn't switch off."
He had been seconded from the Ministry of Defence to the Cabinet Office for a job in global terrorism, handling first-hand intelligence from GCHQ, MI5 and MI6.
Leaving his Whitehall office one Monday evening, he swept up a pile of forms to fill in to make his secondment official.
Back at home, he realised that buried within the bundle were "two papers on two classified subjects, and they were both top secret".

Why is Elon Musk plotting a mega-merger of SpaceX and Tesla?
A composite picture shows Elon Musk wearing a blue suit jacket and white shirt next to a photo of a Tesla car and a picture of a SpaceX rocket taking offImage source, Getty Images/Reuters
ByOsmond Chia
Business reporter
Published
21 October 2026, 05:13 BST

Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together.
Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."
The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.
With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.
Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.
How likely is the merger?
"In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group.
The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said.
Musk, chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects.
Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations.
The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers.

The Hongwu Emperor (21 October 1328 – 24 June 1398), personal name Zhu Yuanzhang, was the founding emperor of the Ming dynasty of China, reigning from 1368 to 1398. Born into a peasant family in Anhui, Zhu grew up amid famine, epidemics, and unrest under the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty. Orphaned at 16, he briefly lived as a novice monk before joining the Red Turban rebels in 1352. Rising rapidly, he captured Nanjing in 1356, established a regional regime, and defeated rival rebels. In 1368, he proclaimed the Ming dynasty, adopted the era name Hongwu, and expelled the Yuan from China proper. During his 30-year reign, he restored stability after decades of war, strengthened state institutions, promoted agriculture, and maintained a disciplined army while seeking to limit civilian suffering. Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together.
Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."
The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.
With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.
Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.

Richard Jackson with a beard and short hair wearing a navy blue hoodie with you are enough written on it in white. He has a neutral expression and there is a fence and foilage behind him.Image source, Maddie Birch-Jackson
Image caption,
Former civil servant Richard Jackson made headlines in 2008 when he left top secret files on a train
ByJennifer Meierhans
Published

Warning: This story contains a reference to suicide
It was an ordinary Tuesday train ride to work when top civil servant Richard Jackson made the biggest mistake of his life. By the time he realised, with a sudden jolt of panic, it was too late.
He had left highly classified documents on the train.
The split-second error became national news and Jackson's life was thrown into turmoil. He was consumed by shame and humiliation.
Nearly 20 years on, he recounts that fateful day and the aftermath, speaking to Dr Sian Williams for BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast. He says he is proof that even when you've made your worst mistake you can rebuild your life.
Before his life unravelled, Jackson was 37 and living in Yateley in Hampshire with wife Maddie and stepdaughter Charlotte, 15. His other stepdaughter Becky, 20, was at university.
"We were very happy," he says. "But I was very focused on my career.
"My worth and my value came from that career, job title, position and responsibility.
"I found myself working 100-hour weeks for a while," he says. "I didn't switch off."
He had been seconded from the Ministry of Defence to the Cabinet Office for a job in global terrorism, handling first-hand intelligence from GCHQ, MI5 and MI6.
Leaving his Whitehall office one Monday evening, he swept up a pile of forms to fill in to make his secondment official.
Back at home, he realised that buried within the bundle were "two papers on two classified subjects, and they were both top secret".

The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.

Hackers steal children's data after company used 'Password1' to protect old account
A close-up of a woman's hand typing on a computer keyboard in the dark against colourful lights in background. The keyboard is lit up.Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Hackers stole information from Data Cymru's systems in 2024 which exposed the personal information of 3,300 people
ByAngharad Thomas
BBC Wales
Published
1 hour ago
A cyber-attack stole information belonging to thousands of children by accessing an account that used the password "Password1", a data watchdog has said.
The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and Data Cymru after the attack on 1 November 2024.
The hackers exposed personal information belonging to 3,300 people, mostly children, by using a test account, known as Test2, which had existed for more than 12 years and was protected by the password that could be compromised in less than a second.
ONL said the account "should have been removed long before criminals were able to use it", adding it had brought in independent cyber-security specialists.
The company, which provided IT services to Data Cymru, said it accepted the ICO's findings and had "acted on them".
Data Cymru merged with the Welsh Local Government Association (WLGA) in 2025, who said there was no evidence the stolen information was "shared further or misused".
ONL and Data Cymru were found to have breached UK GDPR rules, external by failing to properly protect their systems and by not regularly checking whether their security measures were effective.
During the ransomware attack, the hackers encrypted 182.7GB of data and stole 42GB from Data Cymru's systems. It exposed the personal information related to two projects supporting children and families.
David Doodson, head of investigations at the Information Commission's Office, said: "Password1 is not an appropriate password, it is a wide-open door to nefarious actors.

History of the software¶
Python was created in the early 1990s by Guido van Rossum at Stichting Mathematisch Centrum (CWI, see https://www.cwi.nl) in the Netherlands as a successor of a language called ABC. Guido remains Python’s principal author, although it includes many contributions from others.
In 1995, Guido continued his work on Python at the Corporation for National Research Initiatives (CNRI, see https://www.cnri.reston.va.us) in Reston, Virginia where he released several versions of the software.
In May 2000, Guido and the Python core development team moved to BeOpen.com to form the BeOpen PythonLabs team. In October of the same year, the PythonLabs team moved to Digital Creations, which became Zope Corporation. In 2001, the Python Software Foundation (PSF, see https://www.python.org/psf/) was formed, a non-profit organization created specifically to own Python-related Intellectual Property. Zope Corporation was a sponsoring member of the PSF.

The International Bureau of Weights and Measures (French: Bureau international des poids et mesures, BIPM) is an intergovernmental organisation (IGO), through which its 67 member-states act on measurement standards in areas such as chemistry, ionising radiation, physical metrology, as well as the International System of Units (SI) and Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).[2][3] It is headquartered in the Pavillon de Breteuil in Saint-Cloud, near Paris, France. The organisation has been referred to as IBWM (from its name in English) in older literature.[note 1]
Function
The BIPM has the mandate to provide the basis for a single, coherent system of measurements throughout the world, traceable to the International System of Units (SI). This task takes many forms, from direct dissemination of units to coordination through international comparisons of national measurement standards (as in electricity and ionising radiation).[5]

Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding has launched a new prize aimed at discovering funny diary writers from the north of England, saying opportunities across the UK are "very uneven".
West Yorkshire-born Fielding, who penned Bridget's famous diary as well co-writing the film adaptations, has set up the Bridget Jones Prize, external with charity New Writing North.
The award will go to the person who submits the funniest 1,000-word piece of first-person writing.
Speaking at an event for the Independent, which first published Bridget's diary in 1995, Fielding said the spread of opportunity for writing in the UK is "very uneven", adding: "There's much more opportunity in the south than in the north, where I grew up."
The winner of the new prize - set to run for an initial three years from 2027 to 2029 - will receive a £2,000 prize and a package of writing support from Fielding's literary agents and New Writing North.
Fielding's original newspaper column went on to be published as a best-selling novel titled Bridget Jones's Diary in 1996.
It spawned several sequels and hit movie adaptations starring Renée Zellweger as the endearingly chaotic and lovelorn thirty-something diarist.

I left state secrets on the train - I'm proof you can recover from the biggest mistake of your life
Richard Jackson with a beard and short hair wearing a navy blue hoodie with you are enough written on it in white. He has a neutral expression and there is a fence and foilage behind him.Image source, Maddie Birch-Jackson
Image caption,
Former civil servant Richard Jackson made headlines in 2008 when he left top secret files on a train
ByJennifer Meierhans
Published
21 October 2026, 00:05 BST
Warning: This story contains a reference to suicide
It was an ordinary Tuesday train ride to work when top civil servant Richard Jackson made the biggest mistake of his life. By the time he realised, with a sudden jolt of panic, it was too late.
He had left highly classified documents on the train.
The split-second error became national news and Jackson's life was thrown into turmoil. He was consumed by shame and humiliation.
Nearly 20 years on, he recounts that fateful day and the aftermath, speaking to Dr Sian Williams for BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast. He says he is proof that even when you've made your worst mistake you can rebuild your life.
Before his life unravelled, Jackson was 37 and living in Yateley in Hampshire with wife Maddie and stepdaughter Charlotte, 15. His other stepdaughter Becky, 20, was at university.
"We were very happy," he says. "But I was very focused on my career.
"My worth and my value came from that career, job title, position and responsibility.
"I found myself working 100-hour weeks for a while," he says. "I didn't switch off."
He had been seconded from the Ministry of Defence to the Cabinet Office for a job in global terrorism, handling first-hand intelligence from GCHQ, MI5 and MI6.
Leaving his Whitehall office one Monday evening, he swept up a pile of forms to fill in to make his secondment official.
Back at home, he realised that buried within the bundle were "two papers on two classified subjects, and they were both top secret".

Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together.
Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."
The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.
With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.
Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.

Musk, chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects.
Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations.

The International Bureau of Weights and Measures (French: Bureau international des poids et mesures, BIPM) is an intergovernmental organisation (IGO), through which its 67 member-states act on measurement standards in areas such as chemistry, ionising radiation, physical metrology, as well as the International System of Units (SI) and Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).[2][3] It is headquartered in the Pavillon de Breteuil in Saint-Cloud, near Paris, France. The organisation has been referred to as IBWM (from its name in English) in older literature.[note 1]
Function
The BIPM has the mandate to provide the basis for a single, coherent system of measurements throughout the world, traceable to the International System of Units (SI). This task takes many forms, from direct dissemination of units to coordination through international comparisons of national measurement standards (as in electricity and ionising radiation).[5]
Following consultation, a draft version of the BIPM Work Programme is presented at each meeting of the General Conference for consideration with the BIPM budget. The final programme of work is determined by the CIPM in accordance with the budget agreed to by the CGPM.[6][7]

A fifth foreign company has pulled out of a plan to build a cable car from West to East Jerusalem that threatens to involve the seizure of land and property rights from dozens of Palestinian families along its route, but local authorities insist the scheme is proceeding as planned.
The project appeared to have stalled for four years until late September, just weeks before Israel’s 27 October elections, when the Jerusalem Development Authority (JDA) issued a notice of intent to award a contract without a public tender to ROPES, a cable car engineering consultancy based in South Tyrol, Italy.
However, Stephan Obexer, chief executive of ROPES told the Guardian his company had declined the consultancy work because of another commitment in India.
The 1.4km cable car route, approved by the Israeli government in 2019 and upheld by the high court in 2022, would connect West Jerusalem to a planned 16,000 sq metres tourist complex promoted by Elad, a settler organisation seeking to consolidate Israeli control over Palestinian areas of occupied East Jerusalem.

snippet:
Extending and Embedding the Python Interpreter¶
This document describes how to write modules in C or C++ to extend the Python interpreter with new modules. Those modules can do what Python code does – define functions, object types and methods – but also interact with native libraries or achieve better performance by avoiding the overhead of an interpreter. The document also describes how to embed the Python interpreter in another application, for use as an extension language. Finally, it shows how to compile and link extension modules so that they can be loaded dynamically (at run time) into the interpreter, if the underlying operating system supports this feature.
This document assumes basic knowledge about C and Python. For an informal introduction to Python, see The Python Tutorial. The Python Language Reference gives a more formal definition of the language. Python built-ins reference documents the built-in functions and object types, and The Python standard library documents the modules (both built-in and written in Python) that give the language its wide application range.
For a detailed description of the whole Python/C API, see the separate Python/C API reference manual.
To support extensions, Python’s C API (Application Programmers Interface) defines a set of functions, macros and variables that provide access to most aspects of the Python run-time system. The Python API is incorporated in a C source file by including the header "Python.h".
Note
The C extension interface is specific to CPython, and extension modules do not work on other Python implementations. In many cases, it is possible to avoid writing C extensions and preserve portability to other implementations. A police officer wearing black uniform and turquoise gloves takes swabs from a green school gate, which is surrounded by blue and white police tape.Image source, Shaun Whitmore/BBC

ByRobby Westat King's Lynn Crown Court and Lewis Adams
Published
21 October 2026, 11:44 BST
Updated 40 minutes ago
A teenage boy who had a hatred of women and an "obsessive interest" in killers has been found guilty of the attempted murder of a girl at his school.
The boy dressed in black and wore a face mask before stabbing the 15-year-old victim in the back at Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, in March.
Armed police were called to the school, which went into lockdown, and the attack was caught on CCTV.
The boy, who is 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, wrote notes about hating women and had an "obsessive and dangerous interest in killers and killing", jurors at King's Lynn Crown Court were told. He will be sentenced on 18 December.
Jurors deliberated for just under four hours before delivering a majority verdict at the end of a trial which began two weeks ago.
The teenager "went to school not to learn, but to kill" while armed with a kitchen knife, the prosecution said.
The school went into lockdown after the attack and there was an armed police response, while the girl was taken to hospital with a minor injury.

title: Katie Boulter: British number two wins in under an hour to reach Japan Open quarter-finals - BBC Sport
snippet:
Boulter wins in under an hour to reach quarters
Katie Boulter in a blue outfit and cap, with her racket held near her head after playing a shotImage source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Katie Boulter is British number two after Sonny Kartal replaced her at the top of the rankings on Monday
ByMike Peter
BBC Sport journalist
Published
4 hours ago
Katie Boulter moved into the quarter-finals of the Japan Open after she beat Viktorija Golubic in less than an hour.
The British number two defeated her Swiss opponent 6-2 6-1 in Osaka and will face either Croatia's Antonia Ruzic or American Kayla Day in the next round.
Boulter saved a break point in the opening game but dominated from 2-2 in the first set, winning nine games in a row before Golubic took the penultimate game of the match.
The 30-year-old lost the British number one spot to Sonny Kartal on Monday, but is set to retake the position following her run this week.
Boulter, who is seeded eighth in the competition, said she was pleased with how she handled "difficult conditions", with a strong wind affecting play.
"I think one of the biggest things for me is staying patient in the wind," she said.
"Sometimes I can get a little frustrated, and I'm very pleased that I didn't allow that to affect me today and I think I ended up playing some really good tennis in the second set. I'm really pleased with the performance."

Israeli police detain 10 people in rare raid against West Bank settlers
Move comes after US photojournalist and group of European diplomats and Palestinians were assaulted in separate attacks
Mon 19 Oct 2026 19.05 BST
Last modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 16.13 BST
Share
Israeli police have detained 10 people in a rare raid against settlers, after a weekend of extreme violence in the occupied West Bank including an attack on US photojournalist Heidi Levine, which she described as an “attempted lynching”.
She was knocked down, kicked and beaten by a group of masked Israeli men as she covered the olive harvest in a Palestinian village on Friday. The militants broke four vertebrae and a rib, ripped open her finger so it required surgery and left her with lacerations across her body.
“I was practically, basically lynched by a gang of Jewish settlers in the area of Ramallah,” Levine said, in an interview with the BBC from her hospital bed on Monday.
The day after that assault, Israeli militants armed with sticks and iron bars attacked a group of European diplomats and Palestinians harvesting olives outside the town of Taybeh, assaulting a visiting French mayor, smashing the window of an official car, and causing severe injuries to a young Palestinian man.
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, questioned the accounts of Israeli militant violence, ignoring extensive video and witness evidence.
He referenced an “alleged attack” on Levine, whose severe injuries were visible in interviews from her hospital bed, and “unproven allegations” the diplomats had been targeted by militants.

I left state secrets on the train - I'm proof you can recover from the biggest mistake of your life
Richard Jackson with a beard and short hair wearing a navy blue hoodie with you are enough written on it in white. He has a neutral expression and there is a fence and foilage behind him.Image source, Maddie Birch-Jackson
Image caption,
Former civil servant Richard Jackson made headlines in 2008 when he left top secret files on a train
ByJennifer Meierhans
Published
21 October 2026, 00:05 BST
Warning: This story contains a reference to suicide
It was an ordinary Tuesday train ride to work when top civil servant Richard Jackson made the biggest mistake of his life. By the time he realised, with a sudden jolt of panic, it was too late.
He had left highly classified documents on the train.
The split-second error became national news and Jackson's life was thrown into turmoil. He was consumed by shame and humiliation.
Nearly 20 years on, he recounts that fateful day and the aftermath, speaking to Dr Sian Williams for BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast. He says he is proof that even when you've made your worst mistake you can rebuild your life.
Before his life unravelled, Jackson was 37 and living in Yateley in Hampshire with wife Maddie and stepdaughter Charlotte, 15. His other stepdaughter Becky, 20, was at university.
"We were very happy," he says. "But I was very focused on my career.
"My worth and my value came from that career, job title, position and responsibility.
"I found myself working 100-hour weeks for a while," he says. "I didn't switch off."
He had been seconded from the Ministry of Defence to the Cabinet Office for a job in global terrorism, handling first-hand intelligence from GCHQ, MI5 and MI6.
Leaving his Whitehall office one Monday evening, he swept up a pile of forms to fill in to make his secondment official.
Back at home, he realised that buried within the bundle were "two papers on two classified subjects, and they were both top secret".

Business reporter

Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together.
Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."
The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.
With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.
Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.
How likely is the merger?
"In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group.
The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said.
Musk, chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects.
Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations.
The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers.

title: They hear, but do they care? What AI can teach us about listening better
snippet:
They hear, but do they care? What AI can teach us about listening better
20 January 2026
Emily Kasriel
Estudio Santa Rita Brightly coloured illustration of a man sitting down gesturing with his hand while talking and chatbot windows overlayed on the scene (Credit: Estudio Santa Rita)Estudio Santa Rita
AI chatbots don't interrupt and aren't judgemental – so what can they teach us about deep listening?
"I am aware it's a machine but it's super convenient and knows how to listen well whenever I need it," says Anna, a Ukrainian living in London. She is talking about her regular use of the premium version of ChatGPT, a chatbot powered by artificial intelligence.
What Anna – the BBC is not using her real name to protect her identity – finds particularly valuable isn't necessarily the AI's advice, but its ability to give her space for self-reflection.
"I have a history with it, so I can rely on it to always understand my issues and communicate with me in a way that suits me," she says. She is aware that this might seem odd to many people, including her friends and family, which is why she has asked to remain anonymous.
But when she recently broke up with her boyfriend she found the AI's patient listening offered something that her protective friends and family couldn't provide with their immediate judgments about her ex-partner – "he's an idiot".
Instead, the absence of judgement created an opportunity for self-understanding as she unpacked her mixed emotions.
And Anna is not alone: recent Harvard Business Review research shows that in 2025 therapy and companionship was the single most common use of generative AI through the family of tools like ChatGPT, which can carry out a conversation much like a person.

title: Christina Applegate says she was wrongfully diagnosed with MS
snippet:
Christina Applegate says she was wrongly diagnosed with MS
17 hours ago
Brandon Drenon
AFP Christina Applegate pictured wearing a black top and smiling towards the cameraAFP
Christina Applegate thought she was living with multiple sclerosis (MS) for five years, until recently discovering she had been given a wrong diagnosis.
The actress, known for hits like Anchorman and Married With Children, said she was "not happy at all" about the news and in tears when she found out.
"You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said in an episode of her Messy podcast released on Tuesday. "If anything, I've gotten worse."
The two-part episode, co-hosted by Jamie Sigler, ends a recent break she took to process the information. An investigation into what has been causing her debilitating symptoms - which she experiences daily - will begin next week.
"I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me," she said.
In the podcast, Applegate said that "all of a sudden, a few years ago", her doctor suggested ending her infusion treatment for MS to see how her body reacted.
During the time off, her body did not respond in a way that would indicate she had MS.
Doctors then looked into her case further and concluded she did not have the autoimmune disease, which can cause muscle stiffness and problems with walking and talking.
"She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,' " Applegate said, recalling the moment.
"I was, like, not happy at all," she continued. "Everybody else was so happy."
Misdiagnoses can be extremely distressing for people dealing with chronic illnesses, said Dr Michael Kornberg.
"It becomes part of your identity," the associate professor of neurology at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine said, noting how there is a "comfort" in knowing what is happening inside your body.
"To live with that for five years and then to be given a different diagnosis is really unsettling."

Last modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 17.26 BST

A Canadian man was convicted of animal cruelty charges on Monday for snatching a flamingo named Peachy from its enclosure at an iconic Las Vegas hotel.
Prosecutors said it was a malicious prank while a lawyer for the tourist insisted it was drunken foolishness not meant to harm the bird.
Prosecutors said tourist Mitchell Fairbarn hurt and frightened the 27-year-old Chilean flamingo when he took it from its habitat at the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino and carried the squawking bird to his room on 3 March. Defense attorney Josh Tomsheck told jurors at trial in a Nevada court that the man deeply regretted the “bad decisions” he made while intoxicated.
After about five hours of deliberations, jurors returned convictions on felony and misdemeanor animal cruelty counts against the Ontario, Canada, man.
Fairbarn remains under house arrest pending a sentencing hearing set for 1 December. He faces up to four years in prison for the felony and possibly six more months for the misdemeanor conviction. Following the verdict, he declined to comment as he left the courtroom with his wife. He showed no visible emotion.
His lawyer also had no comment.
After the incident, the flamingo was mostly unharmed but is more anxious and nervous when being evaluated, said Peachy’s veterinarian, Tiffany Moore, medical director of Lone Mountain Animal Hospital.

The Hongwu Emperor (21 October 1328 – 24 June 1398), personal name Zhu Yuanzhang, was the founding emperor of the Ming dynasty of China, reigning from 1368 to 1398. Born into a peasant family in Anhui, Zhu grew up amid famine, epidemics, and unrest under the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty. During the time off, her body did not respond in a way that would indicate she had MS.
Doctors then looked into her case further and concluded she did not have the autoimmune disease, which can cause muscle stiffness and problems with walking and talking.
"She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,' " Applegate said, recalling the moment.
"I was, like, not happy at all," she continued. "Everybody else was so happy."
Misdiagnoses can be extremely distressing for people dealing with chronic illnesses, said Dr Michael Kornberg.
"It becomes part of your identity," the associate professor of neurology at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine said, noting how there is a "comfort" in knowing what is happening inside your body.
"To live with that for five years and then to be given a different diagnosis is really unsettling."

Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding has launched a new prize aimed at discovering funny diary writers from the north of England, saying opportunities across the UK are "very uneven".
West Yorkshire-born Fielding, who penned Bridget's famous diary as well co-writing the film adaptations, has set up the Bridget Jones Prize, external with charity New Writing North.

Speaking at an event for the Independent, which first published Bridget's diary in 1995, Fielding said the spread of opportunity for writing in the UK is "very uneven", adding: "There's much more opportunity in the south than in the north, where I grew up."
The winner of the new prize - set to run for an initial three years from 2027 to 2029 - will receive a £2,000 prize and a package of writing support from Fielding's literary agents and New Writing North.
Fielding's original newspaper column went on to be published as a best-selling novel titled Bridget Jones's Diary in 1996.

Third-quarter GDP up by 4.5% compared with last year as industrial output is buoyed by electronics demand

Roaring exports lifted China’s economic growth in the third quarter of this year, with factory output growing much faster than consumer spending.
China’s GDP grew by 4.5% year-on-year between July and September, the National Bureau of Statistics of China reported on Monday. The figures were better than economists had expected and up from the second quarter’s growth rate of 4.3%.
China’s economy has now grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year, putting it on track to hit the government’s 2026 target of 4.5%-5% growth without extra stimulus measures.
Industrial production rose 5.5% in September, up from 5.2% in August, while retail sales only increased 1.1%, up from 0.4%.
Duncan Wrigley, the chief China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said Beijing’s policymakers were likely to conclude that their efforts to stabilise headline growth in the third quarter were successful.
“Headline industrial production rose in September partly as coalmines resumed operations after safety inspections prompted by a major accident. Manufacturing output growth remained robust at 6.0% year on year in September, buoyed up by stronger export demand for electronics, AI-related equipment and autos,” Wrigley said.

State attorneys general step up plans to counter Trump’s meddling in midterms
Coordination by Democratic officials overseeing elections includes Zoom calls and in-person tabletop exercises
Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.11 BST
Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.13 BST
Share
Democratic state attorneys general, other top state officials and civic groups have accelerated planning to thwart any federal meddling in the November midterm elections by Donald Trump as he continues his false charges of widespread voting fraud and veiled threats of interfering in the process.
Since early this year, 24 Democratic attorneys general have expanded coordination with about a dozen Democratic secretaries of state and several civic groups using weekly Zoom calls and in-person tabletop exercises to strategize about countering any federal intervention in the elections.

The ancient Cappadocian language is an unattested language once spoken in antiquity in Cappadocia, a historical region of central Anatolia in modern-day Turkey. There are no known texts written in Cappadocian, although classical Greek writers identified Cappadocian as distinct from Greek, and a few Greek words were attributed to a Cappadocian origin. The language also influenced the pronunciation of Greek spoken by Cappadocians, whose accent was infamous among classical authors, but there is no evidence for a corresponding influence on Greek grammar or vocabulary.
Although Cappadocian does not have a secure linguistic classification, it likely belonged to the Anatolian branch of the Indo-European languages, probably as a relative or descendant of Luwian. This view is supported by recurring Anatolian elements in personal and place names in Cappadocia and its history as part of the Anatolian-speaking Hittite Empire during the Bronze Age. Prior to the modern understanding of Anatolian languages in the twentieth century, Cappadocian was variously considered part of the Semitic family, part of other known branches of Indo-European, or part of an Anatolian language family unrelated to any other known languages.
Cappadocian became extinct by the sixth century AD when it was fully replaced by Greek. Despite nineteenth-century claims to the contrary, the ancient Cappadocian language has had no demonstrable influence on the Modern Greek dialect of Cappadocian Greek.

The experiment involved three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region. Photograph: Martín Mejía/AP
The experiment involved three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region. Photograph: Martín Mejía/AP
Giving £2 a day to people in the Amazon helps protect rainforest, pilot project finds
Researchers say almost 90% of participants in unconditional basic income scheme in Peru adopted environmentally beneficial practices
Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.00 BST
Last modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.02 BST
Share
A pioneering project to provide Indigenous people in the Peruvian Amazon with an unconditional basic income has contributed to the protection of the rainforest, according to a study.
The analysis from the University of Bath is expected to contribute to a growing debate about the role of direct payments to communities that maintain globally important ecosystems.
A two-year pilot managed by the UK-based charity Cool Earth gave 211 people in three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region six cash transfers of 1,032 Peruvian soles each – roughly equivalent to £2 a day – to spend as they wished.
Over the course of the trial, researchers found almost 90% of participants adopted environmentally beneficial practices, such as collective reforestation, restoration of critical water sources and reductions of forest burning.
They also noted a reduction in food insecurity, which can sometimes prompt forest people to start logging or become involved in environmental crimes. Households unable to afford nutritious food fell from 73% to 26%.
Another reported benefit was reduced migration, with the share of participants forced to leave their homes to find work falling from 43% to 18%. Researchers said this allowed more people to remain and protect the forest.
Dr Nick Langridge, a co-author of the report, said: “The findings suggest that when communities have greater security and autonomy, they are better able to protect the ecosystems they depend on.”

The government has approved drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.
The decision - which comes after years of debate and legal challenges - will pave the way for gas to be extracted from it and used in Britain's gas network within weeks.
BBC Verify has looked at what this means for energy bills, energy security and the environment.
Where is Jackdaw and how much gas is there?
Jackdaw is a gas field 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen. It is owned by Adura Energy, which is itself equally owned by the energy companies Shell and Equinor.
The owners of the site, which was first approved four years ago but subject to legal delays until now, estimate Jackdaw has around 10 million cubic metres of recoverable gas., external
Based on official forecasts, external for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.
Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.

Where does Britain currently get its gas from?
Around half of the UK's natural gas comes from its existing North Sea gas fields and is pumped ashore via pipelines.
Gas imports, external make up the remainder. Of these, most come from Norway's North Sea gas fields via separate pipelines.

Introduction

Key Points
All links on the BBC Public Service site or on the editorial pages of a BBC Commercial site must be editorially justifiable
Audiences need to be confident that our decisions on using links and feeds are influenced neither by political or commercial pressures, nor by any personal interests
A link must never be included on the Public Service site or within the editorial content of a commercial site in return for cash, services or any other consideration in kind.
An external site which is a candidate for a link should, generally, be relevant to the BBC content from which a link is envisaged and meet the expectations of the likely audience.
The producer must check the contents of the external site before adding a link to a BBC page.
BBC sites which cover matters of controversy or public policy may offer links to external sites which, taken together, represent a reasonable range of views about the subject.
For programme support pages, an external link should be justified by the relevance and value of the material to the programme's audience.
When linking to any commercial site, great care must be taken to avoid giving the impression that the BBC is endorsing a commercial product or service.
Links from individual pages on the Public Service site to the BBC's Commercial sites are acceptable only when clearly editorially justified.

snippet:
Author Helen Fielding launches award to find the next Bridget Jones's Diary
Renée Zellweger (left) and Helen Fielding pictured together while attending the Bridget Jones Scenes in the Square statue unveiling at Leicester Square, London in 2025Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding (right) alongside film star Renée Zellweger
ByPaul Glynn
Culture reporter
Published
1 hour ago
Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding has launched a new prize aimed at discovering funny diary writers from the north of England, saying opportunities across the UK are "very uneven".
West Yorkshire-born Fielding, who penned Bridget's famous diary as well co-writing the film adaptations, has set up the Bridget Jones Prize, external with charity New Writing North.
The award will go to the person who submits the funniest 1,000-word piece of first-person writing.
Speaking at an event for the Independent, which first published Bridget's diary in 1995, Fielding said the spread of opportunity for writing in the UK is "very uneven", adding: "There's much more opportunity in the south than in the north, where I grew up."
The winner of the new prize - set to run for an initial three years from 2027 to 2029 - will receive a £2,000 prize and a package of writing support from Fielding's literary agents and New Writing North.
Fielding's original newspaper column went on to be published as a best-selling novel titled Bridget Jones's Diary in 1996.
It spawned several sequels and hit movie adaptations starring Renée Zellweger as the endearingly chaotic and lovelorn thirty-something diarist.
'Comedy heart'
In a statement announcing the prize, external, Fielding noted how the "comedy heart" of Bridget's story came from the "everyday humour of people around me when growing up in Yorkshire: laughing together at our mess-ups; bringing the fancy and pretentious down to earth".

title: I left state secrets on the train - I am proof you can recover from the biggest mistake of your life - BBC News
snippet:
I left state secrets on the train - I'm proof you can recover from the biggest mistake of your life
Richard Jackson with a beard and short hair wearing a navy blue hoodie with you are enough written on it in white. He has a neutral expression and there is a fence and foilage behind him.Image source, Maddie Birch-Jackson
Image caption,
Former civil servant Richard Jackson made headlines in 2008 when he left top secret files on a train
ByJennifer Meierhans
Published
21 October 2026, 00:05 BST
Warning: This story contains a reference to suicide
It was an ordinary Tuesday train ride to work when top civil servant Richard Jackson made the biggest mistake of his life. By the time he realised, with a sudden jolt of panic, it was too late.
He had left highly classified documents on the train.
The split-second error became national news and Jackson's life was thrown into turmoil. He was consumed by shame and humiliation.
Nearly 20 years on, he recounts that fateful day and the aftermath, speaking to Dr Sian Williams for BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast. He says he is proof that even when you've made your worst mistake you can rebuild your life.
Before his life unravelled, Jackson was 37 and living in Yateley in Hampshire with wife Maddie and stepdaughter Charlotte, 15. His other stepdaughter Becky, 20, was at university.
"We were very happy," he says. "But I was very focused on my career.
"My worth and my value came from that career, job title, position and responsibility.
"I found myself working 100-hour weeks for a while," he says. "I didn't switch off."
He had been seconded from the Ministry of Defence to the Cabinet Office for a job in global terrorism, handling first-hand intelligence from GCHQ, MI5 and MI6.
Leaving his Whitehall office one Monday evening, he swept up a pile of forms to fill in to make his secondment official.
Back at home, he realised that buried within the bundle were "two papers on two classified subjects, and they were both top secret".
